status_summary: Several parts are operative, one is blocked in court, and the anti-fraud item is unverified. In 2025 the Attorney General overruled two Garland-era decisions: Matter of S-S-F-M- (decided 2025-09-02) overruled the 2021 Matter of A-B- III, and EOIR's decision index also lists Matter of R-E-R-M- & J-D-R-M- (A.G. 2025) overruling the 2021 Matter of L-E-A- and Matter of Negusie (A.G. 2025) restoring the 2020 Negusie decision; no review of every Garland-era decision was found. Two rules revive 2020 rules: a DHS and DOJ rule of 2025-12-30 (90 FR 61035) let the public health provisions of the December 2020 Security Bars and Processing rule take effect on 2025-12-31 while withdrawing its credible-fear and third-country amendments, and the Board of Immigration Appeals appellate-procedures interim final rule of 2026-02-06 (91 FR 5267) adopts measures from the 2020 appellate rule; on 2026-03-08 the U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia granted partial summary judgment setting aside the substantive parts of that interim rule (per a court-docket summary), and the case is stayed pending a final rule. EOIR statistics generated 2026-07-24 show pending cases at 3,469,569 at the end of the third quarter of fiscal 2026, down from 3,722,776 at the end of fiscal 2025, with 662 immigration judges on board against 735 at the end of fiscal 2024; EOIR announced 47 more judges sworn in on 2026-09-24. DOJ moved to terminate the Flores settlement on 2025-05-22 and the district court denied the motion on 2025-08-15. The Civil Rights Division's Immigrant and Employee Rights Section lists employer settlements from 2025-09-29 through 2026-08-04 and a suit filed 2026-04-28 over excluding U.S. workers. The Ninth Circuit heard the government's appeal of the Flores denial (Flores v. Blanche, No. 25-6308) on 2026-06-02, and no decision was found through 2026-10-17; on 2026-08-18 the district court appointed a Special Master and Independent Monitor under the settlement.

timeline.event: A federal district judge in Los Angeles denies the Justice Department's motion (filed 2025-05-22) to terminate the Flores settlement, calling it a repeat of the 2019 attempt.

The Attorney General issues Matter of S-S-F-M- (29 I&N Dec. 206 and 207), overruling Matter of A-B- III (2021); the EOIR decisions index for volume 29 also lists Matter of R-E-R-M- & J-D-R-M- (A.G. 2025), overruling Matter of L-E-A- (2021), and Matter of Negusie (A.G. 2025), vacating a stay so that the 2020 Negusie decision is operative.
DHS and EOIR publish a final rule confirming the 2025-12-31 effective date of the December 2020 Security Bars and Processing rule and withdrawing parts of it that conflict with later rules.

EOIR publishes an interim final rule making Board of Immigration Appeals merits review discretionary, shortening most appeal deadlines to 10 days and adopting briefing measures from the 2020 appellate rule (effective 2026-03-09).

In Amica Center for Immigrant Rights v. EOIR (D.D.C., No. 1:26-cv-00696), the court granted partial summary judgment, set aside the substantive parts of the appellate interim final rule (presumptive summary dismissal, the 10-day appeal deadline and the waiver provisions) and remanded; on 2026-04-10 the case was stayed on the parties' stipulation pending a final rule (per a court-docket summary).

The Ninth Circuit heard argument in Seattle in Flores v. Blanche, No. 25-6308, the government's appeal of the district court order denying its motion to terminate the 1997 Flores settlement agreement (calendar listing; argument reported by Bloomberg Law the same day).
EOIR statistics generated this day show 3,469,569 pending cases at the end of the third quarter of fiscal 2026 and 662 immigration judges on board (53 temporary judges as of 2026-06-30).
EOIR proposes a rule defining immigration judges' contempt authority and setting a civil money penalty process for contempt.

In Flores v. Blanche (C.D. Cal., No. CV 85-4544-DMG) the district court discharges its order to show cause and, by Docs. 1827 and 1828, appoints a Special Master and Independent Monitor for CBP and ICE facilities for an initial 12 months (orders read on a copy posted by plaintiffs' counsel).
